78: Beef is calculated, not assumed. The calculator in the kit starts from an 80/20 blend (a mix of cuts for the ground beef: chuck, brisket and short rib) bought already ground at the kit estimate of $5.25 per lb, and with the end-of-day shrink that comes to $5.41 per usable lb. Whole chuck ground in house comes to $5.15 per usable lb before the labor of cleaning and grinding it, and the "Beef & Patty" tab tells you how much that labor can cost before grinding stops paying: about $0.26 per usable lb. A pound gives about 5.3 balls of 3 oz (85 g) raw, or about 5.2 once you count the end-of-day shrink. At about 1.6 balls per cover, the case needs about 58.5 lb of beef a day, which sizes the daily order. The costing always goes on the price before sales tax: with the kit's default values a single costs $2.00, about 24% of its price, and a double costs $3.21, about 29%, with American cheese at about $0.14 a slice and a potato bun at $0.55. A 5 oz portion of frozen fries comes to $0.46 and a fresh-cut one to $0.35 before labor, the oil adds about $0.10 a portion, and the "Costing" tab puts the whole week, weighted by what sells, at about 26%. The plan uses frozen fries: fresh-cut is a brand decision, not a cost one.
79: The equipment is bought with a price and a source. A 36" gas flat-top (the commercial steel griddle) runs from $589 to $4,858 on WebstaurantStore depending on the range, and the case's two 48" flat-tops with the bun toaster and the smash presses come to {{inv_plancha}}; smash presses are sold as aluminum burger presses at $10.49-25.99. The three gas fryers with filtration and the fry station come to {{inv_freidoras}}: the third fryer is for breaded chicken, so the fries are not cooked in the same oil. The Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression costs {{inv_campana}}, and the exhaust duct with makeup air, {{inv_conducto}}. The make line, with the refrigerated chef base and the cheese and holding station, comes to {{inv_montaje}}; the walk-in cooler, reach-ins, freezer and ice machine, {{inv_frio}}, with the raw beef at 41 °F (5 °C) or below; the shake machine and the beverage station, {{inv_batidos}}. The exhaust duct is the most delicate line of the space: get a quote before you sign the lease.
80: Craft rules the flat-top, and what follows is a guide: the flat-top at 400-450 °F, about 90 seconds on the first side and 60 on the second. It is not a substitute for the cooking rule, which is a safety rule and is set in section 9. The hours of the case run seven days a week, 11:00 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. (11:00 p.m. on Friday and Saturday), and the kitchen opens at 8:30 a.m. Production is done before opening, about 2.5 hours a day: portioning the balls, making the sauces, cutting the toppings and restocking the make line, the refrigerated station where every burger is built. With that done, during service the flat-top only smashes, flips and plates, and the build never stops. If you leave production until there is already a line, the flat-top waits on the make line and the counter jams.
81: Hygiene goes inside the operation, not next to it. Raw beef lives in the walk-in or the reach-in at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (Food Code 3-501.16), stored below ready-to-eat food and apart from other meats (3-302.11). Season the ball on the flat-top, not hours ahead. If you grind in house, grind only what the day needs. Spatulas, scrapers and trays for raw beef stay apart from those for cooked food, and the cut toppings and sauces stay at 41 °F (5 °C) or below with date marking. Every batch of balls is checked with a probe, one smash per batch, to 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds. The fryer runs at 350-355 °F with the color guide in view; the oil is filtered every night and changed by TPM (total polar materials) or by the manufacturer's guidance, with each change logged, and the used oil goes to a licensed renderer. The Burger Joint Checklists Kit Pro from AI Chef Pro has the sheets for the flat-top, the fryers, the make line and delivery.
82: You need two beef suppliers, each with its own specification: the blend, the 80/20 ratio, and the supplier's establishment number plus the lot and date on every invoice. Add a bun supplier, potato buns with their allergens, and the fries with their sheet. The prices of beef, buns, cheese and fries are a kit estimate: confirm them with your suppliers. Utilities average {{suministros_mes}} a month, between the gas for the flat-tops, the electricity of the fryers, the hood, refrigeration and air conditioning. Maintenance is a separate line: hood and duct cleaning, the flat-tops and the gas lines, the fryers and the refrigeration. Waste and used oil are another line of their own.
85: The team of the case is short, with seven rows on the "Staffing" tab. You are the owner and the general manager: you buy the beef, choose the blend and the suppliers, approve the menu and the food safety plan, run the flat-top at the busy service and manage the marketplaces, and your pay is set below what a chain manager would earn, so think of an owner's draw in addition from net profit. With you are a shift lead, who runs the line during service; two grill cooks, who smash every ball and bring out the crust; a fry and prep cook; three part-time counter crew, who work the register, the expo and the to-go packing; three part-time weekend crew; and one person for dish and prep. Everyone is paid at least $15 an hour, there are no servers and no tip credit, and the tips from the tip jar or the POS belong to the team.
86: With relief for vacations and days off, the table adds up to {{plantilla_puestos}} people, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas_xl}} full-time equivalents, and costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1 including employer payroll taxes of {{cargas_pct}}, or {{personal_pct}} of sales. Hours coverage is {{cobertura_horas}}. But the annual schedule hides a detail: on Friday and Saturday nights you need more people, with two on the flat-top, one on the fryers and the make line, someone at the order counter, someone packing to-go orders and someone at the expo. Put it in the shift schedule. A single grill cook who can run the flat-top is a risk, not a saving: if that person is out, the flat-top does not run. Staff grows with people, not with a percentage.
87: Pay every employee at least the highest of the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour, according to the Department of Labor, or {{salario_minimo_federal}} a year for a full-time employee at {{horas_semana}} hours a week), your state's and your city's, and remember that many are well above it. The case budgets at least $15 an hour and does not model a tip credit. The tips from the tip jar or the POS belong to the team, as your state allows; the owner and the managers never keep tips. Hourly employees get overtime above 40 hours a week under the FLSA. Give every hire an offer letter, complete Form I-9 and Form W-4 on day one, and keep accurate time records in the POS. Your accountant or payroll provider confirms which rules apply to you.
88: The flat-top is the bottleneck, so the grill cook is the key hire. In job listings, a cook who can run a flat-top asks for clearly more than counter crew, so budget above the minimum for that seat. Hire the person who will run the flat-top before the build-out, and ask for an opinion on the line and the refrigeration. One more warning: never replace staff with independent contractors who invoice you and work your schedule. That is worker misclassification, and the IRS and the Department of Labor treat it as a violation that can bring back taxes and penalties.
89: If you ever want your own delivery driver, in most states that person has to be a W-2 employee, and you will need hired and non-owned auto insurance. That is why the case has no in-house delivery: marketplace orders are delivered by the marketplace itself, and the weekend crew is for the flat-top and for packing to-go orders. Before putting a driver on the payroll, do the math with your own orders (in the case, about 19 marketplace orders a day): it is a fixed cost, while the marketplace charges its commission of {{comision_pct}} only when you sell.
90: Train the team before you open. At least one Certified Food Protection Manager must be on site (Food Code 2-102.12), and many states also require food handler cards for the rest of the team; the training has to cover ground beef, the probe, the fryer oil, allergens and cross-contact. The line also needs its own training: the ounces of the ball, the smash and the build, so weigh ten balls from each person. On top of that, OSHA covers burns from the flat-top and the fryers, slips on grease, cuts and lifting. The HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro from AI Chef Pro helps you write the food safety plan your training follows.
93: To open you need {{inversion_total}}. That is {{capex}} for build-out, kitchen, refrigeration, hood, equipment and opening, which includes the security deposit and {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before opening, plus {{fondo_maniobra}} of working capital. The largest lines are the build-out ({{inv_obra}}), the refrigeration ({{inv_frio}}), the flat-tops ({{inv_plancha}}) and the hood ({{inv_campana}}). The cash needed at opening is {{necesidad_caja}}. The funding is {{fondos_propios}} of your own money and a {{prestamo}} SBA 7(a) loan at {{tipo_prestamo}} over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, with no interest-only period and an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax is collected from guests and passed on to the state, so it never enters the investment.
94: The three-year income statement projects sales of {{ventas_a1}}, {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}. The gross margin of year 1 is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, after all variable costs: goods ({{cogs_pct_xl}} of sales), disposables ({{consumibles_pct}}), the marketplace, card fees ({{tarjeta_pct}}) and a contingency. Labor adds up to {{personal_a1}} ({{personal_pct}} of sales), rent to {{ocupacion_anual}} ({{ocupacion_pct}}), and prime cost, goods plus labor, is {{prime_cost_pct}}. Earnings before depreciation and interest are {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}}. Net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}, with a net margin of {{margen_neto_a1}} in year 1; the model taxes profit at an effective {{impuesto_beneficios}} income tax rate, and your own rate depends on your structure, so confirm it with your accountant. Be honest about food cost: the plan carries food at {{food_cost_comida}}, the prudent side, because it counts the consumption of the whole menu, with waste, comps, chicken, bacon and shakes, while the theoretical costing of the calculator comes to about 26% weighted. The gap is what gets lost between the recipe and the register: balls, buns and sauces thrown away at close, staff meals, mistakes, marketplace refunds and promotions, and a beef price that moves.
95: The growth is what the Excel does: covers grow {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{clientes_dia}} to {{clientes_a2}} and {{clientes_a3}} a day, at the same average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, and staff grows with people, not with a percentage. On taxes, the workbook uses an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}}, a single rate, which is collected from guests and never counted as revenue; menu prices with tax come to {{precio_menu}} on average. Some states tax to-go food differently, so check yours. Food and beverage you buy for resale are usually bought under a resale certificate without sales tax, so your accountant should confirm how your state treats purchases, packaging and equipment.
96: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, with revenue of {{equilibrio_ventas}}. Cash break-even, which also covers the loan payments, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day, with revenue of {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}}, and it leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over the plan. With no interest-only period you repay principal from the first month, so that margin already includes the loan, and it is the number to watch every year. The case asks for {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day with take-out and delivery covers included, across {{aforo}} seats. Counted in the dining room alone, without the orders that leave the building, the turns are lower, which is why pickup and delivery are part of the plan and not an extra.
97: The cash flow numbers the months from 1 to 12, and Month 1 is January, in calendar order. The ramp-up starts below the cruising pace and reaches it in four months, in April, which is why working capital counts. The lowest balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, falls in Month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}, January, when the ramp-up has barely started. February is the slowest month, May is a peak with National Burger Month and graduations, June, July and August follow, and the fall is steady. In a resort or beach town the summer climbs: change the weights in the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab.
98: The minimum DSCR is {{dscr_min}}: the business covers its debt with room to spare. Payback before debt comes from the cash flow: {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone. Recovery depends on the flat-top delivering every day: this is a craft business, not an annuity. If the numbers do not work, the lever is the menu price, never more debt.
99: The pessimistic scenario is a weak year: {{pesimista_clientes}} covers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}, still a profit, but a thin one. In the optimistic one, {{optimista_clientes}} covers at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days give sales of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. Every point of food cost on food sales takes about 1% of food sales straight out of profit, and the price of beef is the risk of the case: a rise of $0.75 per lb adds about $0.28 to a double. Check the price of beef every four weeks, measure your real usage (food purchases divided by food sales for the month) in the first quarter and change the cell. The Excel rules, and if you change a green cell, this document stays behind.
102: Most owners open as an LLC, which you file with your state, and many add an operating agreement; talk to your CPA about LLC versus S corp taxation. Then get an EIN from the IRS and register for a sales tax permit with your state. In the US, requirements stack in layers: federal, state, county and city, and each one has its own forms. Apply for the city or county business license and, before you sign anything, run a zoning check on the exact address for restaurant use and the hood. Submit your plans for plan review with the health department (Food Code 8-201.11 asks for plans before construction or remodeling), then get your building permit and, at the end, the certificate of occupancy, with the fire marshal's sign-off. The workbook uses an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}}, a single rate; some states tax to-go food differently, so check yours.
103: Fire and the hood come first. A Type I hood with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air goes over the flat-tops and the fryers, with a Class K extinguisher nearby, and the hood and the duct are cleaned under NFPA 96: quarterly with heavy grease, twice a year if moderate, so ask the fire marshal. Plan for a grease interceptor, which your county sizes in the plan review, and have the gas lines installed by a licensed plumber or gas fitter with a permit. Before the health permit you will have a pre-opening inspection, with the walk-in, the reach-ins and the make line cold at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. The Food Code asks for a Certified Food Protection Manager on site (2-102.12), and many states also require food handler cards for the rest of the team. The fryer oil is filtered every night and changed by TPM or by the manufacturer's guidance, since there is no federal limit on polar materials, and the used oil goes to a licensed renderer.
104: Ground beef is the sensitive point. Under the FDA Food Code 2022 (3-401.11(A)(2); each state adopts its own edition), ground beef must be cooked to 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds, or 145 °F (63 °C) for 3 minutes, 150 °F (66 °C) for 1 minute or 158 °F (70 °C) instantly. The SOP of the kit is that every smash burger reaches at least 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds, checked with a thin-tipped probe on one sample per batch; the color and the crust do not certify the temperature. Chicken goes to 165 °F (74 °C). Raw beef is held at 41 °F (5 °C) or below (3-501.16), below ready-to-eat food and apart from other species (3-302.11). Buy the beef already ground, or in balls, with the supplier's establishment number and the lot and date on file. As for grinding logs, the FSIS rule (9 CFR 320.1(b)(4)) covers retail stores and official establishments that grind raw beef, and this kit does not claim it is mandatory for a restaurant; if you grind in house, keep a house-grind log as good practice (lots, establishment numbers, the date and time of each grind and of each cleaning) and ask your health department.
105: The consumer advisory (3-603.11) applies only if you offer a burger cooked to order, at the guest's request (3-401.11(D)). It has two parts, a disclosure ("hamburgers (can be cooked to order)" or an asterisk) and a reminder ("Consuming raw or undercooked meats, poultry, seafood, shellfish, or eggs may increase your risk of foodborne illness"), and it goes on the menu, the website and your marketplace listings. It never applies to the kids' menu or to highly susceptible populations (3-801.11). The case serves everything cooked through and needs no advisory. On acrylamide, the compound that forms when potatoes and bread brown at high heat, there is no federal limit for restaurants. California Prop 65 is another matter: the state sued several chains over acrylamide in fried potatoes in 2005, and KFC agreed in 2007 to warn customers and pay $208,000 plus $133,000. If you open in California, ask your attorney about the Prop 65 warning for fried potatoes.
106: The nine major allergens are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, peanuts, tree nuts, wheat, soy and sesame, which was added in 2023 under the FASTER Act. In a smash burger, the bun carries wheat, milk, egg or soy depending on the recipe, and sesame in the seeds and sometimes in the oil; American cheese is milk; sauces such as mayo are egg; shakes are milk, and their mix-ins can carry peanuts or tree nuts; the breaded chicken sandwich is wheat, egg and milk; and the shared fryer oil is where cross-contact happens. A shared flat-top passes wheat and sesame to the beef if you toast the bun on it. Mustard is not a major allergen in the United States, though it is in the UK. Do not promise "gluten-free" (21 CFR 101.91). Make an allergen matrix by dish before opening and review it whenever you change a supplier or a sauce.
107: The beer license, or beer and wine license, comes from a state agency plus local approval. Apply early and never count on it. Liquor liability goes in your insurance, together with general liability, product liability for the beef, property and workers' comp, which come to {{seguros_anual}} a year in the case. Staff are W-2 employees paid by the hour, never 1099 for grill cooks or counter crew, with Form I-9 and Form W-4 on day one. There are no servers and no tip credit: the tips from the tip jar belong to the team, and the managers and the owner never keep tips. Add music licenses (ASCAP, BMI and SESAC) and check local packaging ordinances, because some cities ban polystyrene.
108: Selling burgers from your home kitchen is another matter. There is no federal rule, and state cottage food laws do not cover raw beef, a TCS food, so this plan assumes a permitted restaurant, and you should check your state before you try anything else. This section lists what we can state with confidence; for everything else, check with your accountant, your city or the health inspector before you decide. A note for UK readers: register your food business with your local council at least 28 days before you open and expect a Food Hygiene Rating of 0 to 5; the FSA expects burgers made from minced beef to be cooked thoroughly unless validated controls are in place, so ask your local authority. VAT is 20% on dine-in and on hot take-away food (check HMRC VAT Notice 709/1). There are 14 allergens to declare, including mustard, celery, sulphites, lupin and molluscs, and a premises licence plus a personal licence if you sell alcohol. In Australia, you need a Food Safety Supervisor and GST is 10%.
111: The conclusion is that a neighborhood smash burger restaurant of this size is viable, but demanding. With {{clientes_dia}} covers a day at {{ticket}} per equivalent cover, excluding sales tax, the first year leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}} and a cash margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}}, with the loan payments already in. The minimum DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, the lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in January, and payback before debt is {{payback}} with the working capital reserve counted in the investment, and {{payback_capex}} on startup costs alone. It is a craft business, sustained by a busy flat-top every day, and it is not for going in with tight capital.
112: These are the thirteen mistakes of a burger restaurant and how to avoid them. The first is trusting your eyes: the color and the crust do not certify the temperature, so probe one smash per batch to 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds. The second is offering a burger cooked to order without the consumer advisory, or without deciding before you open: if you offer it, the disclosure and the reminder (3-603.11) go on the menu, the website and every marketplace listing. The third is buying or grinding beef with no paper trail: keep the supplier's establishment number and the lot and date on file, and if you grind in house, keep a house-grind log and never mix lots. The fourth is storing raw beef above ready-to-eat food or above 41 °F (5 °C): raw goes below, apart from other species, and cold.
113: The fifth is frying too hot and changing the oil when it smells: the fryer runs at 350-355 °F, and the oil is filtered every night and changed by TPM or by the manufacturer's guidance, with each change logged. The sixth is one fryer for fries and breaded chicken, and then calling the fries "gluten-free": never promise it, and give the breaded chicken its own fryer to keep cross-contact down. The seventh is a marketplace with no ceiling. The commission, the promotions and the cash take the margin, and a smash burger travels worse than it looks, with the fries suffering most: that is why the ceiling of the plan is {{plataforma_pct}} of sales.
114: The eighth is pricing the menu without costing by channel: a combo leaves $12.07 dine-in, $11.52 take-out and $9.12 through a marketplace, so the margin falls by about a quarter when it goes out by delivery. Cost every channel with the calculator before you set the menu. The ninth is a long menu, with bun and ingredient waste you end up throwing away: a short menu speeds up service, cuts waste and makes it easier to measure the real food cost. The tenth is depending on a single beef supplier with no specification for the blend: having two, with the sheet and the establishment number and lot on every invoice, is the insurance of the flat-top.
115: The eleventh is getting sales tax wrong: some states tax to-go food differently, so confirm the rule for your state and set the rate in your POS before you open. The twelfth is copying the investment of a franchise for a 1,700 sq ft space: it is good for comparing, not for budgeting your own case. And the thirteenth is opening with no schedule for Friday and Saturday nights, when the flat-top is the bottleneck: the schedule with a bigger crew at night is made before opening. If you keep only one mistake, make it the beef: the beef that is ground, held or cooked wrong is what puts the guest and the business at risk. Almost all of these mistakes have a task in the checklist, placed in the order in which it pays to do it.
116: The action plan has six phases and 80 tasks in the checklist that comes with the kit. "Phase 1 - Business Setup" has 12 tasks. "Phase 2 - Hood & Permits" has 15. "Phase 3 - Beef & Health" has 14. "Phase 4 - Staff & Allergens" has 13. "Phase 5 - Menu, Brand, Delivery" has 13. And "Phase 6 - Opening & 90 Days" has 13. Follow the order: the zoning check and the fire marshal's answer on the hood and the duct come before you sign the lease, the beer license application goes in as soon as you do, and the grill cook who will run the flat-top is hired before the build-out. Decide before you open whether you offer burgers cooked to order, and file the establishment number and lots of each beef supplier. Check off each task when you close it, and if one slips, see what depends on it before you move the opening date.
117: The next step is to fill in the Excel with your own numbers: your real rent, your average check, your covers, your loan, your staff and your opening calendar. Change only the green cells; this document reflects the example case, and yours is set by your spreadsheet. Then, with the Smash Burger Patty, Fries & Costing Calculator, weigh ten balls, measure the cook loss on the flat-top and the fries portions per lb, and in the first quarter compare your actual food cost with the {{food_cost_comida}} in the plan. For the sheets of the flat-top, the fryers, the make line and delivery, use the Burger Joint Checklists Kit Pro, and for the costing of the whole menu, the Food Cost Kit Pro. And if what attracts you is a different format, the burger truck has its own Food Truck Business Plan Kit.
